- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.11) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if followed by a spike.
- If sentiment shows strong negative spikes (e.g., -0.28 or lower), model often underestimates downward moves; increase forecast low by 5–10% to account for sentiment-driven sell-off.
- Model frequently overreacts to recent price spikes (e.g., 73+), producing exaggerated upward momentum; cap 30d forecast slope at 1–2% per day after a 70+ spike.
- When sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (0.06–0.11), model often fails to capture mean reversion; adjust forecast to align with 18-day moving average if deviation >3%.
- If sentiment history shows alternating positive/negative cycles, model tends to lag in direction; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead if sentiment is trending, or delay if sentiment is reversing.
- For 30d forecasts, if true outcome shows early sharp decline (first 5–7 days), model often misses it; add 2–3% downward bias in first 5 days if sentiment is negative.
- If sentiment is stable or flat (0.00–0.06), model tends to overfit recent trends; apply smoothing filter or reduce forecast volatility by 15–20% to avoid overfitting.
